results.title: 10 Stratified Sampling Examples (2026)
results.content: **Stratified sampling is a sampling method in scientific research that involves ensuring your sample group has fair representation of sub-groups (strata) of a population you’re studying. To do this, you ensure each sub-group of the population is proportionately represented in the sample group.**. For example, if you have a population of 50,000 people in a city and you want to survey them, you probably can’t survey them all. But you’ll want to ensure the sample group (those 100 people you survey) truly represent the city population as a whole. This, in essence, is stratified sampling: ensuring each sub-group (or ‘strata’) in your sample is represented in the correct portion to the entire population. results.title: Stratified Sampling: How to Reduce Sampling Bias with Case Studies
results.content: # How can you use stratified sampling to reduce sampling bias in your population? What are some case studies of stratified sampling? One way to reduce sampling bias is to use stratified sampling, a technique that divides your population into subgroups based on relevant characteristics and then selects a proportional or equal number of units from each subgroup. In this article, you will learn how to use stratified sampling and see some case studies that illustrate its benefits and challenges. ## 1 What is stratified sampling? Stratified sampling involves creating strata, or homogeneous subgroups, based on one or more variables that are related to your research question or hypothesis. When using stratified sampling, you create subgroups based on certain characteristics of your population, such as age, gender, income, or education level. ## 2 Why use stratified sampling? Stratified sampling can help you reduce sampling bias and increase the accuracy and efficiency of your analysis. Stratified sampling can also help you compare and contrast the characteristics and outcomes of different subgroups within your population. Here’s where Stratified sampling can help you achieve this by reducing sampling bias and increasing the accuracy and efficiency of your analysis. By stratifying your sample, you can ensure that each subgroup is adequately represented in your analysis, and you can avoid oversampling or undersampling certain groups that might skew your results. Stratified sampling also has some drawbacks, such as requiring prior knowledge and information about your population and the variable or variables that you want to use to create your strata. ## 6 What are some case studies of stratified sampling? They divided their population into four strata based on age and selected a proportional sample from each stratum using simple random sampling. (2019) divided their population into two strata based on school type and selected an equal sample from each stratum using cluster sampling. (2018) divided their population into four strata based on income level and selected a proportional sample from each stratum using systematic sampling. Through these studies it was found that stratified sampling can help to uncover the impact of certain interventions as well as the influence of certain variables on consumer preferences and attitudes.

results.title: Ways to Avoid Sampling Bias in Surveys - SmartSurvey
results.content: Ways to Avoid Sampling Bias in Surveys. # Ways to Avoid Sampling Bias in Surveys. Sampling bias is something that can easily creep into surveys when the methods used unwittingly favor certain outcomes over others. ## What is Sampling Bias? Sampling bias, also referred to as sample selection bias, refers to errors that occur in surveys and research studies when participants are not accurately selected. Preferably you should select your online survey participants at random. ### A famous example of Sampling Bias from yesteryear. By failing to properly examine the population sample that owned telephones during this era, the researchers conducting the telephone survey committed sampling bias, resulting in severely skewed response data. Rather than distribute a survey to a sample that more accurately represented the population of the United States, the researchers ended up with inaccurate and unrepresentative insights, which failed to predict Truman, as the eventual winner of the presidential race. ## How to avoid Sampling Bias. ### More tips to combat Sampling Bias in your surveys. #### Simple Random Sampling. The great thing about simple random sampling is that no effort is required on the part of your potential participants. #### Stratified Random Sampling. Another technique that can be used to avoid sampling bias is stratified random sampling. Using this approach, those conducting the survey will be able to examine the population they will be working with in their study and comprise an accurately representative sample accordingly. For example, stratified random sampling is effective if there are 1,000 individuals in a population and 10 people from the population are required to conduct a study. Stratified random sampling helps researchers become aware of this information prior to building their sample, to help ensure they avoid sampling bias. If you are about to create a fresh survey and want the best chance of avoiding sampling bias, you may like to revisit some of the advice and ideas we have discussed in this blog post. It’s also important to consider that no matter how long you may have been in the survey creation business, sampling bias is something that can be committed by even the most experienced professionals.
